title: Multimodal Search
shortDefinition: Retrieval that spans multiple content types — text, images, audio, and video — using a shared embedding space.
definition: Multimodal search is retrieval that spans multiple content types — finding images using a text query, finding similar images to an uploaded photo, retrieving documents based on an image description, or searching across text and video in a single query — by embedding different modalities (text, images, audio) into a shared vector space where cross-modal similarity can be measured. Where standard vector search compares text to text or image to image, multimodal search allows any-to-any retrieval across content types.
introduction: Multimodal search is retrieval that spans multiple content types — finding images using a text query, finding similar images to an uploaded photo, retrieving documents based on an image description, or searching across text and video in a single query — by embedding different modalities (text, images, audio) into a shared vector space where cross-modal similarity can be measured. Where standard vector search compares text to text or image to image, multimodal search allows any-to-any retrieval across content types.

sections.title: How multimodal search works
sections.description: Embedding models map different content types into a shared vector space for cross-modal similarity comparison.

content.text: Multimodal search relies on embedding models trained to map different content types — text and images most commonly — into the same vector space, where semantically related content from different modalities clusters together regardless of type. CLIP (Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training) from OpenAI is a foundational example: a model trained to align images and their text descriptions in a shared embedding space, enabling text queries to retrieve related images and image queries to retrieve related text. More recent vision-language models extend this alignment across additional modalities and with greater precision.

items: Shared embedding space — different modalities mapped to the same space.
Cross-modal similarity — semantically related content clusters together.
CLIP — foundational model for text-image alignment.
Vision-language models — extend alignment across more modalities.
Any-to-any retrieval — text, image, audio, and video all comparable.

content.title: The key insight
content.text: Multimodal search enables any-to-any retrieval across content types — text queries find images, images find documents, and more.

sections.title: Common business applications of multimodal search

content.text: E-commerce product search — customers upload a photo of a product they want and receive results of similar items, or search using natural language descriptions that match product images. Media asset management — searching a library of images, videos, and documents using natural language rather than requiring manual tagging of every asset. Medical imaging — retrieving similar patient images or matching images to textual clinical notes. Manufacturing quality control — finding historical defect images similar to a newly captured defect for reference. Content moderation — retrieving similar policy-violating content from a library when a new violation is detected.

sections.title: Limitations and risks of multimodal search

content.text: Multimodal search has limitations. Cross-modal retrieval quality can be lower than within-modal retrieval. Embedding models for less common modalities (audio, video) are less mature than text-image models. The quality depends on the embedding model and its training data — domain-specific content may underperform. Multimodal search requires appropriate model selection and validation. Indexing diverse content types adds infrastructure complexity. The performance gap between different modality pairs should be validated for each use case.

items: Cross-modal quality gap — often lower than within-modal retrieval.
Modality maturity — audio and video models are less mature.
Domain dependency — performance varies by content type and domain.
Infrastructure complexity — indexing multiple modalities adds overhead.
Validation requirement — cross-modal performance must be measured.
Model selection — choosing the right embedding model is critical.

content.title: Important
content.text: Cross-modal retrieval quality can differ significantly from text-to-text or image-to-image retrieval. Validate performance on your specific use case before scaling.

faqs.title: Frequently asked questions about multimodal search

items.question: Can multimodal search handle queries like 'show me images similar to this' from an uploaded photo?
items.answer: Yes — image-to-image retrieval using shared embedding space is a core multimodal search capability.

items.question: Which content types does multimodal search currently support?
items.answer: Text and image are most mature and widely available; audio and video are increasingly supported but typically at lower retrieval quality than text-image; ClickMasters evaluates current model capabilities against your specific modality requirements.

items.question: Does multimodal search require separate indexes for each content type?
items.answer: In a shared embedding space architecture, all modalities share a single vector index — a text query and an image query both produce vectors in the same space that can be compared against all indexed content.

items.question: How large can a multimodal search index get?
items.answer: Vector databases supporting multimodal search scale to millions of items; ClickMasters sizes infrastructure for your specific content volume and growth trajectory.

items.question: How long does building a multimodal search system take?
items.answer: 12–28 weeks depending on modality complexity and content volume.

items.question: Can multimodal search be combined with keyword or metadata filtering?
items.answer: Yes — hybrid search combining cross-modal vector retrieval with metadata filtering (category, date, author) is common and often improves precision.

items.question: What is the difference between multimodal search and multimodal AI?
items.answer: Multimodal AI is the broader field of AI that processes multiple modalities. Multimodal search is a specific application — retrieval across modalities. Multimodal search is built on multimodal AI capabilities.

items.question: What embedding model is commonly used for multimodal search?
items.answer: CLIP (OpenAI) is a foundational text-image embedding model. Other options include Cohere's multimodal models, Google's multimodal embeddings, and open-source models like SigLIP. ClickMasters selects the right model for your use case.

items.question: Can multimodal search handle video content?
items.answer: Yes — video can be processed as sequences of frames or as full video embeddings. Video retrieval capabilities are less mature than image retrieval but improving rapidly. ClickMasters evaluates video options based on your requirements.

items.question: How do you evaluate multimodal search quality?
items.answer: Using standard retrieval metrics (precision@k, recall) on representative cross-modal queries. ClickMasters builds evaluation frameworks for your specific use case.
